h1: Beer with Sindhi food from sai bhaji to koki
title: Beer with Sindhi Food and Sai Bhaji | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer pairings for Sindhi food: sai bhaji, koki, dal pakwan, Sindhi curry, seyal phulka and aloo tuk, with the beer styles that suit each.
teaser: Sindhi food is hearty, tangy and full of fried treats. It is quietly one of the best cuisines in India for beer.
standfirst: Sindhi cooking brings greens with lentils, crisp fried breads and tangy gram flour curries. Here is how we would match beer to a Sindhi meal, from breakfast koki to Sunday Sindhi curry.
sections: Comfort food built on greens, gram flour and frying

Sindhi food came to Indian cities with families who moved from Sindh after 1947. It is now home cooking in Mumbai, Ulhasnagar, Ahmedabad, Pune and beyond. It is homely and generous: leafy greens cooked down with dal, flatbreads cooked crisp and gram flour used in curries and snacks.

For beer, that means a lot of earthy, savoury flavours, some sourness from tamarind and tomato and plenty of fried textures. Moderate chilli. Not much cream. That opens the door to a wide range of styles, from crisp lagers to brown ales, without the heat problems of some regional cuisines.
Sai bhaji suits a malty amber

Sai bhaji is spinach cooked with chana dal and vegetables such as dill, brinjal, potato and tomato, mashed into a thick, green, savoury dish. It is usually eaten with rice or phulka.

It is earthy and mildly tangy, with dill giving it a herbal note. An amber lager or a Vienna lager at 18 to 25 IBU brings toasty malt to meet the lentils without drowning the greens. If you like ales, an English bitter at around 4% ABV, with its gentle earthy hop character, is a quiet, sensible match. Avoid very roasty beers: spinach and dark roast can taste metallic together.
Koki is the beer snack nobody talks about

Koki is a thick, crisp flatbread made with wheat flour, chopped onion, green chilli, coriander and pomegranate seeds, cooked slowly with ghee or oil. It is a breakfast staple, usually with yoghurt, pickle or tea.

If you ever have koki for a late brunch or a snack, it loves beer. A Helles or a Kölsch, both soft and bready, picks up the toasted wheat. A hefeweizen is the fun option, its own wheat character mirroring the bread. Carbonation of around 2.5 volumes in a lager cuts the ghee neatly.
Dal pakwan and the fried snacks

Dal pakwan pairs a crisp fried flatbread with a mild chana dal topped with onion, tamarind chutney and green chutney. Aloo tuk, potatoes fried, pressed flat and fried again, then sprinkled with masala, is the classic Sindhi side or snack.

Fried and salty is the easiest pairing territory there is. A crisp Pilsner at 25 to 40 IBU works brilliantly, with its bitterness cutting the oil and its bubbles resetting the palate after the sweet and sour chutneys. A pale ale also works with aloo tuk, where the potatoes can stand up to more hop character. For more ideas with fried and chaat style dishes, see our guide to beer with street food.
Sindhi curry needs a crisp partner

Sindhi curry is a tangy gravy made by roasting gram flour in oil, then cooking it with tamarind, tomato and vegetables such as drumstick, okra, potato and cluster beans. It is a Sunday dish, eaten with rice and often with aloo tuk on the side.

The roasted besan gives a nutty depth, while the tamarind gives a sharp sour edge. A Märzen or a brown ale picks up the roasted gram flour. A Belgian witbier answers the sourness with citrus. We lean to the witbier when the curry is very sour and to the Märzen when it is rich with vegetables.
Seyal phulka, seyal mani and meat dishes

Seyal dishes reuse leftover phulka or bread, cooked again in a tomato, onion and garlic masala. Sindhi homes also cook mutton and fish, such as Sindhi style fried fish or mutton cooked with onion and spices.

For seyal dishes, a Helles or amber lager is comfortable. With a mutton curry, a dunkel or a brown ale at 4.5 to 5.5% ABV brings nutty malt to the gravy. Our Indian food and beer pairing guide explains the reasoning behind matching malt depth to meat dishes.

Sweets are part of the meal too. Sindhi homes make sweet lolo (a sweetened flatbread) and the famous Sindhi halwa. Most beers struggle with very sweet desserts, because sugar makes beer taste thinner and more bitter. If you want to try, pick a beer that is at least as sweet as the dish, such as a milk stout at 4 to 6% ABV with sweet lolo. Otherwise, finish the beer with the curry and enjoy the sweets with tea.

If you are hosting, pour a Pilsner with dal pakwan and aloo tuk, an amber lager with sai bhaji and a witbier with Sindhi curry. Serve them all at 4 to 7 °C, since none is a beer that needs warmth to open up. Keep pours small and offer a jaljeera or nimbu pani for anyone not drinking.

Then do one honest test: taste sai bhaji with the Pilsner and with the amber. You may find the Pilsner makes the spinach taste greener and slightly bitter, while the amber makes it taste sweeter. Both are fine. Knowing which you prefer and why is what sensory training is for.

Your first step: make or order koki this weekend and try a piece with a Helles. It may become your favourite beer snack.
faqs: What beer goes with sai bhaji?
An amber lager, Vienna lager or English bitter. Toasty malt meets the lentils without overpowering the greens.
A crisp Pilsner. Its bitterness cuts the fried pakwan and its carbonation resets the palate after tamarind chutney.
Does beer work with Sindhi curry?
Yes. A witbier answers the tamarind sourness with citrus, while a Märzen picks up the roasted gram flour.
